native_result.query: In what centuries did we see the highest growth phase of the period between 2000 BCE and 1100 BCE?
native_result.HypoA: Between 1500 BCE and 1300 BCE, highest growth of the period between 2000 BCE and 1100 BCE is seen.
native_result.HypoB: The highest growth phase of the 2000–1100 BCE window occurred in the 15th–14th centuries BCE (1500–1300 BCE), with the single strongest century being the 15th century BCE (1500–1400 BCE). Based on the study-defined growth rate pollen_grate_100 (percentage change of the 100-year smoothed pollen openness score), the per-century mean growth rates peak at +0.001889 for [1500,1400) BCE and remain elevated at +0.001114 for [1400,1300) BCE — the two top-ranked, contiguous centuries — while all other centuries in the window are at or below +0.000859 and mostly negative (e.g., 17th c. +0.000172, 16th c. −0.003005, 13th c. −0.000167, 12th c. −0.001036). A cross-check with the mean KDE growth rate of the full archaeological record (g_all_mean) independently ranks the same two centuries first (+0.0028293 and +0.0014507). Thus the data support a hypothesis that the region experienced its most sustained openness/agricultural growth in the mid-second millennium, specifically the 15th and 14th centuries BCE.
native_result.WorkflowB: Loaded data/time_series_data.csv (3,601 rows, CE −4100…−500, 1-year resolution, no gaps in the 2000–1100 BCE window; all indicator columns 100/100 per century bin). Computed the arithmetic mean of pollen_grate_100 over the 100 annual rows in each half-open century bin [−2000,−1900)…[−1200,−1100). Identified the peak century as argmax of the century means and the sustained phase as the maximal contiguous run of positive, top-3 century means containing the peak. Cross-checked with per-century means of g_all_mean. Full per-century table in evidence; script saved as analysis.py.
